title: The death of Blessed Frances d'Amboise
shortBlurb: The widowed Duchess of Brittany, who had planted the first Carmel of nuns in France, laid down her rule and died in her own cloister at Nantes…
body: Born about 1427 at the castle of Thouars, Frances was the daughter of Louis d'Amboise, Viscount of Thouars. Betrothed as a small child to Peter, a younger son of John V, Duke of Brittany, she was married at fifteen in 1442. When Peter came to rule as Peter II in 1450, the pair were crowned in the cathedral of Rennes, and her charity so marked his short reign that chroniclers called it "the time of the blessed duchess."

Widowed and childless in 1457, she withstood the pressure of her family and of King Louis XI, who wished her to marry again, and turned instead to God. With Blessed John Soreth, prior general of the Carmelites, she founded in 1463 at Bondon near Vannes the first convent of Carmelite nuns in France, called "The Three Maries," its first sisters brought from Liège. She took the habit in 1468, was elected prioress in 1473, and later made a second foundation at Nantes.

She died on 4 November 1485 near Nantes and was long venerated as the foundress of the French Carmel. Pope Pius IX confirmed her cult in 1863, and her feast is kept on 4 November; images show her in the Carmelite habit with an ermine cloak to recall her rank.

title: The first Catholic diocese in the United States
shortBlurb: By the brief Ex hac apostolicae, Pope Pius VI made Baltimore the first see of the young republic and gave John Carroll to its scattered Catholics…
body: After the American Revolution the Catholics of the new United States had no bishop of their own. The clergy of Maryland and Pennsylvania, unwilling to remain a mere mission under the Congregation of Propaganda, petitioned Rome for a diocesan bishop, and Pope Pius VI took the unusual step of allowing them, for that first time only, to elect their candidate. Father John Carroll, a former Jesuit who had lived at Baltimore since 1786, was chosen by twenty-four of the twenty-six votes.

On 6 November 1789, by the pontifical brief Ex hac apostolicae, the pope erected the Diocese of Baltimore as the first in the United States, a see that then embraced the whole nation. Carroll was consecrated a bishop on 15 August 1790 in the chapel of Lulworth Castle in Dorset, England, by Charles Walmesley, vicar apostolic of the Western District.

Carroll had already helped found Georgetown in 1789; he held the first American diocesan synod in 1791, invited the English Dominicans, and established the Visitation nuns. In 1808 Pius VII raised Baltimore to a metropolitan archdiocese with the new suffragan sees of Bardstown, Boston, New York, and Philadelphia, so that the Church in the republic had its own hierarchy.

title: The Bolshevik Revolution and the war on religion
shortBlurb: The seizure of Petrograd opened one of the longest and bloodiest persecutions the Christian East had ever endured…
body: On 7 November 1917 — 25 October by the Old-Style calendar Russia then kept — Lenin's Bolsheviks overthrew the Provisional Government and stormed the Winter Palace in Petrograd. Within weeks the new regime turned against religion, decreeing in January 1918 the separation of Church and State and the seizure of ecclesiastical property, and setting in motion decades of official atheism.

The Russian Orthodox Church, which had only that same year restored the Moscow patriarchate under Patriarch Tikhon, saw its monasteries closed, its clergy imprisoned or shot, and its faithful driven underground; Tikhon publicly anathematized the persecutors. The Catholics of the former empire, both Latin and Eastern-rite, shared in the suffering, their bishops and priests among the martyrs and prisoners of the coming years.

The Holy See watched with alarm as the persecution spread with Soviet power. Pope Pius XI, who had served as nuncio in the region, condemned atheistic communism in the 1937 encyclical Divini Redemptoris, warning that it sought "to destroy the social order and to undermine the very foundations of Christian civilization."

sources.text: Pope Pius XI, encyclical Divini Redemptoris (19 March 1937), vatican.va

title: The death of Blessed John Duns Scotus
shortBlurb: The Subtle Doctor, who had forged the classic defense of Our Lady's Immaculate Conception, died suddenly at Cologne…
body: Born about 1266 at Duns in the Scottish Borders, John Duns Scotus entered the Friars Minor and studied and taught at Oxford, Paris, and Cologne. The keenness of his mind won him the title Doctor Subtilis, the Subtle Doctor, and later ages ranked him with Thomas Aquinas, Bonaventure, and William of Ockham among the great theologians of the medieval schools.

His most celebrated achievement was the classic defense of the Immaculate Conception. Where others feared it derogated from Christ's universal redemption, Scotus argued that the most perfect Redeemer would preserve his Mother from original sin from the first instant of her being — a redemption more excellent, not less. The maxim later attached to his school, "potuit, decuit, ergo fecit" (God could do it, it was fitting, therefore he did it), summed up the case that Pius IX would define as dogma in 1854.

Transferred to the Franciscan studium at Cologne about 1307, he died there unexpectedly on 8 November 1308 and was buried in the Minorite church. His sarcophagus bears the verse "Scotia me genuit, Anglia me suscepit, Gallia me docuit, Colonia me tenet." Pope John Paul II beatified him in 1993.

title: The founding of the Redemptorists
shortBlurb: St. Alphonsus Liguori gathered a handful of missioners at Scala to preach Christ to the most abandoned poor, choosing for the day the feast of the Lateran…
body: Alphonsus Maria de Liguori, a Neapolitan advocate turned priest, had been stirred by the plight of the herdsmen and country folk of the hills above the Amalfi coast, who lived almost without knowledge of the Gospel. Resting at Scala in 1730 near the sanctuary of Santa Maria dei Monti, he conceived a company wholly given to preaching missions among the most forsaken.

On 9 November 1732, in the humble oratory of a convent at Scala, with Bishop Tommaso Falcoia presiding at the Mass of the Holy Spirit, Alphonsus and a few companions founded the Congregation of the Most Holy Redeemer — the Redemptorists — under the motto "Copiosa apud eum redemptio," "with him is plentiful redemption." He was thirty-six, and the little band numbered fewer than ten. He chose the day deliberately, for it is the feast of the Dedication of the Lateran, the mother church of the world, a sign of the mission's universal reach.

Among the early members was St. Gerard Majella. Pope Benedict XIV gave the congregation formal approval on 25 February 1749. Alphonsus himself became a bishop and a moral theologian of the first rank, and was later named a Doctor of the Church.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “St. Alphonsus Maria de' Liguori”

title: The death of Cnut the Great
shortBlurb: The Danish king of a North Sea empire, who had walked to Rome as a pilgrim and bargained there for his people, died at Shaftesbury…
body: Cnut, son of Sweyn Forkbeard, became king of England in 1016, of Denmark about 1018, and of Norway in 1028, ruling a broad North Sea realm. Though he had won it by the sword, he governed as a Christian king, bringing internal peace, repairing the churches his armies had once plundered, and endowing monasteries with lands and relics.

At Easter 1027 he journeyed to Rome for the imperial coronation of Conrad II, and there, in the presence of Pope John XIX, he negotiated on behalf of his subjects: reduced tolls and safe passage for English and Danish pilgrims and merchants on the road to Rome, and relief from the heavy fees demanded of English archbishops when they came to receive the pallium. His letter of 1027, sent home from abroad, records these things in his own words.

He died on 12 November 1035 at Shaftesbury in Dorset — "on the second of the Ides of November," says the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle — and was buried in the Old Minster at Winchester. His empire did not long outlive him, dividing among his sons.

title: The death of Pope St. Nicholas the Great
shortBlurb: The last of the three popes surnamed "the Great," who upheld the see of Peter against kings and patriarchs alike, died at Rome…
body: Nicholas I was elected bishop of Rome on 24 April 858, consecrated the same day in St. Peter's in the presence of the Emperor Louis II. Of the whole roll of popes, only three bear in the Annuario the title "the Great" — Leo I, Gregory I, and Nicholas — and he earned it as the most forceful pontiff of the Carolingian age.

He upheld the indissolubility of marriage against Lothair II of Lorraine, who sought to put away his wife Teutberga; he defended the rights of bishops such as Rothad of Soissons against their metropolitans; and he resisted Photius, whose irregular elevation at Constantinople foreshadowed the later schism between East and West. In all these causes he asserted the primacy and the judicial authority of the Roman see over the whole Church.

In Rome he rebuilt and endowed churches and encouraged religious life, keeping himself to a spirit of Christian asceticism. He died on 13 November 867, greatly esteemed by his contemporaries; his cult was reaffirmed by Urban VIII in 1630, and his feast is kept on 13 November.

title: The healing of the Western Schism
shortBlurb: With the consecration of Oddo Colonna as bishop, the Council of Constance sealed the end of the forty-year schism that had rent Latin Christendom…
body: For nearly forty years, since 1378, the Latin Church had been torn among rival claimants to the papacy, until at times three men wore the tiara and Christendom scarcely knew whom to obey. The Council of Constance, opened on 5 November 1414, set itself to end the scandal: it deposed John XXIII and Benedict XIII and received the freely-given resignation of the Roman claimant Gregory XII.

On 11 November 1417 the cardinals and the deputies of the five nations, meeting in conclave, unanimously elected Oddo Colonna, who took the name Martin V in honor of St. Martin of Tours, whose feast fell that day. Being then only a subdeacon, he was ordained deacon on the 12th, priest on the 13th, and consecrated bishop on 14 November 1417 at Constance; he was crowned pope on the 21st.

Recognized by the Church as a whole, Martin V brought the schism to an end and set about restoring the papacy and the Papal States. He soon condemned the conciliarist claim that a general council stands above the pope, forbidding appeal from the pope's judgment in matters of faith, and the long wound of Avignon and the three obediences was at last closed.

title: The Battle of the Winwaed
shortBlurb: By a rain-swollen river in the north, the Christian Oswiu overthrew the pagan Penda, and, Bede says, heathen Mercia turned to Christ…
body: Penda of Mercia, the last great pagan king among the English, had slain the Christian kings Edwin of Northumbria at Hatfield in 633 and Oswald at Maserfield in 642. In 655 he invaded Bernicia at the head of a great confederate host and besieged Bamburgh, threatening to undo the Christian ascendancy of the north.

Oswiu of Bernicia, offering treasure for peace in vain, vowed that if God granted him victory he would dedicate his infant daughter Ælfflæd to perpetual virginity and give twelve estates for the founding of monasteries. On 15 November 655, in the district of Loidis near Leeds, by the river Winwæd swollen with heavy rain, the armies met. Penda and some thirty allied leaders fell, and Bede records that "many more were drowned in the flight than destroyed by the sword."

Bede reckoned the battle the effective end of Anglo-Saxon paganism: Mercia and its neighbours received the Christian faith, and Penda's own baptized son Peada ruled the southern part. Oswiu kept his vow, and his daughter entered the monastery of Abbess Hilda, later removed to Whitby. The exact site of the river is disputed.

sources.text: Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English People, Book III (public-domain translation)

title: The deaths of Mary I and Cardinal Pole
shortBlurb: Within twelve hours the last Catholic queen of England and her Archbishop of Canterbury both died, and with them the Marian restoration…
body: Mary I, daughter of Henry VIII and Catherine of Aragon, had in 1554 reconciled England to Rome and, in 1556, installed the papal legate Cardinal Reginald Pole as Archbishop of Canterbury, the last Catholic to hold that see. Together they sought to undo the breach of the Reformation and to rebuild the old religion in the realm.

On 17 November 1558, about seven o'clock in the morning, Mary died at St James's Palace in London during an epidemic of influenza that ravaged the country. That same evening, about seven o'clock, Cardinal Pole — himself long ill at Lambeth Palace and only just informed of the queen's passing — died as well, nearly twelve hours after his sovereign.

The crown passed at once to Mary's half-sister Elizabeth, who would sever England from Rome again within a year. Pole lay in state at Lambeth and was buried on the north side of the Corona at Canterbury Cathedral. With the deaths of queen and cardinal on a single day, the Catholic restoration in England came to its end.

title: The election of Pope St. Hilarius
shortBlurb: Leo the Great's archdeacon, who had barely escaped the Robber Council of Ephesus, was raised nine days after his master's death to the chair of Peter…
body: Hilarius, a native of Sardinia, had served as archdeacon of the Roman Church and as a legate of Pope Leo I. At the tumultuous Second Council of Ephesus in 449 — the "Robber Synod" that upheld the heresiarch Eutyches — he protested against its violence and fled for his life, afterward standing among the defenders of the Council of Chalcedon.

Nine days after the death of Leo the Great, on 19 November 461, Hilarius was consecrated bishop of Rome. He carried forward his master's policies with vigor, held Roman synods in 462 and 465, and labored to set the churches of Gaul and Spain in order, settling disputes over jurisdiction among their bishops and upholding the discipline of the metropolitans.
In Rome he adorned the churches, and is remembered especially for the oratories he added to the Lateran baptistery. He died on 29 February 468 and is venerated as a saint of the Church.

title: The accession of Diocletian
shortBlurb: On a hill outside Nicomedia the army hailed a Dalmatian officer as Augustus, and the Church of Egypt would one day date its Era of Martyrs from his reign…
body: After the deaths of the emperor Carus and his son Numerian, the army of the East gathered on 20 November 284 on a hill some miles outside Nicomedia in Bithynia. There the officers saluted the commander of the household troops, Diocles, as their new Augustus; he accepted the purple, swore he had no part in Numerian's death, and soon Latinized his name to Diocletianus. He was to reign twenty-one years and then, alone among Roman emperors, to abdicate.

Diocletian restored order after the long anarchy of the third century, reorganizing the empire under the fourfold rule of the Tetrarchy. Yet in 303 he unleashed the Great Persecution, the last and most systematic assault the pagan state ever made upon the Christians, with edicts to destroy the churches, burn the Scriptures, and compel sacrifice.

So many were the martyrs of those years that the Church of Alexandria reckoned its calendar as the "Era of Martyrs" (Anno Martyrum), counting from his accession — a reckoning the Coptic Church keeps to this day. Lactantius, in his account of the deaths of the persecutors, preserves the day of his proclamation.

sources.text: Lactantius, On the Deaths of the Persecutors (public-domain translation)

title: Frederick II is crowned emperor
shortBlurb: In St. Peter's, Pope Honorius III set the imperial crown on his former ward, who vowed a crusade and swore to guard the Church…
body: Frederick II of Hohenstaufen, king of Sicily through his Norman mother and king of Germany through his father Henry VI, had as a fatherless boy been the ward of Pope Innocent III. His old tutor, Cencio Savelli, now reigned as Pope Honorius III and had labored to bring him peacefully to the imperial dignity.

On 22 November 1220 Honorius crowned Frederick Holy Roman Emperor in St. Peter's Basilica at Rome. During the ceremony Frederick took the cross once more, renewing his vow to lead a crusade to the Holy Land, and at the pope's request he promulgated constitutions protecting the rights of the Church and clergy and issued severe edicts against heretics, placing the secular sword at the service of the faith.

The concord did not endure. Frederick's repeated postponement of his crusade and his ambition to rule all Italy would bring him into a long duel with the papacy, and he was excommunicated under Gregory IX and again under Innocent IV, who at Lyons in 1245 declared him deposed. But on this day pope and emperor stood together in seeming amity in the basilica of the Apostle.

title: The martyrdom of St. Chrysogonus
shortBlurb: A Roman martyr whose name the Church still speaks in the Canon of the Mass was beheaded at Aquileia, tradition holds, in the persecution of Diocletian…
body: Chrysogonus, according to his ancient acts, was a Roman Christian and teacher, remembered in tradition as the instructor and support of St. Anastasia of Sirmium during the persecution. When the emperor demanded that all imprisoned Christians be brought to trial, he was taken from Rome to Aquileia in the north of Italy.

Summoned before the tribunal and commanded to sacrifice to the gods for the promise of honors, he answered that he would adore only the true God and that idols were but devils; for this, tradition says, he was beheaded on 24 November, about the year 304, and his body cast into the sea, to be recovered afterward and buried by a priest. The details of his passion are known only through his legendary acts and are held with caution.

His cult, however, is beyond doubt among the most ancient at Rome: his name was inserted into the Canon of the Mass, and a station church, San Crisogono in Trastevere, was raised in his honor. The Roman Martyrology keeps his memory on this day.

title: The Battle of Montgisard
shortBlurb: On St. Catherine's day the leper-king Baldwin IV, with a handful of knights and the Templars, broke Saladin's host near Ramla…
body: In November 1177 much of the fighting strength of the Kingdom of Jerusalem had marched north toward Syria, and Saladin seized the moment to invade from Egypt toward the Holy City, letting his great army disperse to plunder Ramla and Lydda in confidence that no force could withstand him.

The sixteen-year-old King Baldwin IV, though already wasting under leprosy, mustered what men remained at Ascalon, joined by some eighty Knights Templar from Gaza under their master Odo of St Amand and a few hundred knights. On 25 November 1177, the feast of St. Catherine of Alexandria, he had the relic of the True Cross raised before the army and fell upon Saladin's scattered host at Montgisard, near Ramla, before it could form for battle.

The Muslim army was routed and pursued for miles; Saladin fled and reached Egypt on 8 December with but a tenth of his men. In thanksgiving a Benedictine priory dedicated to St. Catherine was built upon the field, and the victory bought the Crusader kingdom a decade's respite. The precise site, perhaps ancient Gezer, is debated.

title: The death of Queen Isabella of Castile
shortBlurb: The queen who completed the Reconquista and sent Columbus westward died at Medina del Campo, and an age of Spanish glory and shadow was set…
body: Isabella I of Castile, born on 22 April 1451 at Madrigal de las Altas Torres, joined her crown to that of Ferdinand of Aragon and so laid the foundation of a united Spain. In 1492 the two sovereigns took Granada, the last Moorish kingdom, ending the long Reconquista, and in that same year sponsored the voyage of Christopher Columbus across the ocean.

A queen of fervent and practical piety, she promoted the reform of the Spanish Church and its religious orders, aided by Cardinal Cisneros. Yet her reign is remembered also for its shadows, told here without gloss: the establishment of the Spanish Inquisition in 1478 and the expulsion of the Jews from her realms in 1492.

Worn by the deaths of her only son John and her daughter Isabella, she withdrew from the cares of government in September 1504. She died a little before noon on 26 November 1504 in the castle of La Mota at Medina del Campo, and was buried, by her own wish, at Granada. A cause for her beatification was in time opened, and she is styled a Servant of God.

title: The death of St. James of the Marches
shortBlurb: The tireless Observant friar who preached the Holy Name across half of Europe and founded charitable lending houses for the poor died at Naples…
body: Born about 1391 at Monteprandone in the March of Ancona, of a poor family named Gangala, he studied law at Perugia, entered the Friars Minor, and formed himself under St. Bernardine of Siena, embracing an austerity so severe that his master had to bid him moderate his fasts. He was ordained about 1420.

With St. John of Capistrano he became one of the great preachers of the Observant reform, journeying on foot through Italy, Germany, Bohemia, Poland, Hungary, and Bosnia. He spread the devotion to the Holy Name of Jesus under the monogram IHS, served as inquisitor and papal legate against heresy, reconciled feuding cities, and promoted the Monti di Pietà — charitable pawnshops that lent to the poor at little or no interest to spare them the usurer.

Sent by the pope in his last years to Naples, he died there on 28 November 1476 and was buried in the Franciscan church of Santa Maria la Nova, his body venerated as incorrupt. Beatified by Urban VIII in 1624 and canonized by Benedict XIII in 1726, he is honored among the patrons of Naples.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “St. James of the Marches”

title: The death of Pope Clement IV
shortBlurb: The French lawyer-pope who counseled Aquinas and Roger Bacon died at Viterbo, and there began the longest conclave the Church has ever known…
body: Gui Foucois, called Guy le Gros, was a married advocate and trusted councillor of St. Louis IX of France. After his wife's death he took holy orders, rose to be bishop of Le Puy, archbishop of Narbonne, and cardinal of Sabina, and was elected pope at Perugia on 5 February 1265, taking the name Clement IV.

He supported Charles of Anjou against the last of the Hohenstaufen, whose cause fell at the battle of Tagliacozzo in 1268, and he was a patron of learning: he protected Thomas Aquinas and urged Roger Bacon to compose his Opus Maius on the sciences. He resided throughout his reign at Viterbo, where he died on 29 November 1268 and was buried at the Dominican church of Santa Maria in Gradi.

The cardinals, divided between French and imperial parties, could not agree on a successor. The Roman see stood vacant for one thousand and six days, until the exasperated people of Viterbo locked the electors in the palace and, it is said, stripped off its roof to hasten them. Gregory X was chosen in 1271, and the scandal gave rise to the law of the enclosed conclave — the cardinals shut up "cum clave," under key.
